text: This study does not support FMT as a salvage therapy in a non-biomarker-driven population of advanced heavily pretreated patients progressing on ICIs. However, the study suggests that FMT can safely be combined with ICI in patients with advanced cancer and that some patients may derive a benefit. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized the treatment landscape in solid tumors and are now standard of care across multiple cancer types.^{1} ICI therapy may offer long-lasting clinical benefit in advanced disease, as demonstrated in melanoma.^{2} Nevertheless, ICI resistance is a challenge, and response rates across all cancers are estimated to be about 20%.^{3} Mechanisms of resistance to ICIs are multifaceted, comprising both tumor cell intrinsic and extrinsic factors, but often not possible to unravel in clinical routine.^{4} Resistance phenotypes include primary resistance, in which tumors do not respond to ICI therapy, and secondary resistance, which implies tumor progression after initial clinical benefit.^{5} The gut microbiota is considered a tumor-extrinsic factor influencing both ICI efficacy6,10 and toxicity,^{11} and is investigated as a potential biomarker in cancer immunotherapy.^{12} Several studies have identified taxa associated with response and resistance to ICIs, but generalizability across different studies has proven difficult.13,15 Further, therapeutic modulations of the gut microbiota are explored, with the aim of enhancing efficacy and improving outcomes.^{16 17} Pioneering clinical trials in melanoma have demonstrated that fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is safe and suggested that a subset of patients with ICI refractory disease may respond after FMT.^{18 19} FMT has also been reported to reverse anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) resistance in gastrointestinal cancers.^{20} Although these early clinical data are promising, the actual benefit of FMT in immuno-oncology is unclear and questions remain about patient selection, choice of ICI backbone, optimal methods of FMT administration and feasibility across different types of cancer.^{21} None of the aforementioned trials included treatment with anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte associated protein 4 (CTLA-4) antibodies. To further address these questions, we designed a single-arm basket trial (MITRIC; NCT05286294) evaluating safety and efficacy of repeated FMTs in patients with ICI refractory disease. The hypothesis was that microbiota modulation by FMT could overcome resistance to ICIs. Here, we report the clinical outcomes as well as translational studies elucidating biomarkers, microbiota engraftment and immunological effects. The MITRIC trial was a single-arm, phase IIa study evaluating the safety, feasibility and efficacy of FMT to patients with cancer with progressive disease on ICI therapy. The study included multiple cancer types, selected based on eligibility for standard ICI therapy and relatively high response rates: Metastatic melanoma, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC; with >20% programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression), clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), non-small cell lung cancer (>20% PD-L1 expression) and microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H)/mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) solid cancers. The key eligibility criteria included disease progression on ICIs, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0–1 and measurable disease according to immunotherapy Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (iRECIST). Prior response to ICIs was allowed, but with disease-specific criteria for the maximum time interval since progression on ICIs. For patients with melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer and MSI-H/dMMR cancer that had received subsequent lines of therapy after ICIs, re-introduction of ICIs and new disease progression was required.
title: Safety and efficacy of fecal microbiota transplantation in solid cancers resistant to immune checkpoint inhibitors: results of the MITRIC trial
